newsitem.title: USA: MCI net hurt by competition, local investments.
newsitem.headline: MCI net hurt by competition, local investments.

text.p: Long-distance carrier MCI Communications Corp. said Wednesday its earnings edged lower in the second quarter, hurt by competition in its core long-distance business and problems in entering local markets.
MCI, based in Washington, reported second-quarter net income of $280 million, or 40 cents a share, down nearly 7 percent from $300 million, or 43 cents a share a year ago.

The results, which were in line with statements the company had made earlier this month regarding its second-quarter performance, matched Wall Street analysts' average estimate of 40 cents a share, according to research firm First Call.
Total revenues rose to $4.8 billion in the second quarter, up 6 percent from the year-ago level of $4.6 billion.
But investments in new ventures and markets reduced second-quarter earnings by $116 million, or 16 cents a share, the company said.
Revenue from MCI's long-distance business reached $4.4 billion, an increase of $195 million, or 4.7 percent, over the second quarter of 1996.
MCI said its plan to target "higher-spending customers," coupled with strong competitive pressures, cut into revenues in the long-distance sector.
The rate of growth in long-distance revenues was the slowest the company has ever reported, analysts said, and compared with the 12.7 percent growth rate MCI posted in the second quarter of 1996.

In the mass-market segment, the company's flagship consumer service, MCI One, rose 50 percent in the last three months, to reach 3 million customers. MCI said 85 percent of new MCI One sales came from non-MCI customers.

MCI's local phone service posted revenues of $80 million, up 82 percent from the second quarter of 1996, but the company said continuing regulatory hurdles to entering U.S. local phone markets hindered growth.

Earlier this month, MCI said anti-competitive practices by local phone companies would result in losses of $800 million in its local business -- double previous estimates -- with the potential for even greater losses in 1998.

MCI has begun offering local phone service in 25 metropolitan regions to date, having launched service in New Jersey only last week. It has said it plans to offer service in at least 31 U.S. local markets by the end of 1997.

MCI has said its local service bid is being impeded by foot-dragging among local Baby Bell operators in opening local markets to competition and by the slow pace of local phone deregulation efforts following the passage of the Telecommunications Act of 1996.
But Chief Financial Officer Doug Maine said Wednesday that MCI remained committed to making hefty investments to enter U.S. local phone markets despite the expected impact on earnings.

"MCI will be among the first long-distance carriers to offer local service nationally," Maine said in a conference call with analysts following the release of the earnings report. "Now is exactly the time to make our move into local."
Last fall, MCI announced its plans to merge with British Telecommunications Plc in a deal worth $21 million.
The proposed union, the largest trans-Atlantic merger ever, is under review by the Federal Communications Commission.

On Monday, FCC Chairman Reed Hundt endorsed the merger plan after the companies assured regulators that British Telecommunications would provide equal access to other companies on its trans-Atlantic phone networks.
MCI's stock fell 37.5 cents to $35.375 in midday trading on Nasdaq.
